extractions.name: Example: Constructing and Solving a Characteristic Equation With Repeated Roots
extractions.problem: Consider the equation $y''-2y'+y = 0.$ If $y = e^{\lambda x}$ is a solution to the equation, then what is $\lambda?$
extractions.worked_solution:
Assuming $y=e^{\lambda x}$ and differentiating $y$ with respect to $x$ gives

$$
y'= \lambda e^{\lambda x},\qquad y''= \lambda^2 e^{\lambda x}.
$$

Substituting the above into our differential equation gives

$$
\begin{aligned}{\lambda }^{2}{e}^{\lambda x}-2\lambda {e}^{\lambda x}+{e}^{\lambda x} & =0 \\ {e}^{\lambda x}({\lambda }^{2}-2\lambda +1) & =0.\end{aligned}
$$

The characteristic equation is therefore

$$
\begin{aligned}{\lambda }^{2}-2\lambda +1 & =0.\end{aligned}
$$

Factoring the auxiliary equation results in

$$
\begin{aligned}(\lambda -1)^{2} & =0\end{aligned}
$$

and so $\lambda =  1$  is a repeated root of the auxiliary equation.

extractions.worked_solution:
Assuming $y={e}^{\lambda x}$ and differentiating $y$ with respect to $x$ gives

$$
{y}^{′}=\lambda {e}^{\lambda x},\,{y}^{″}={\lambda }^{2}{e}^{\lambda x}.
$$

Substituting the above into our differential equation gives

$$
\begin{aligned}{\lambda }^{2}{e}^{\lambda x}+10\lambda {e}^{\lambda x}+25{e}^{\lambda x} & =0 \\ {e}^{\lambda x}({\lambda }^{2}+10\lambda +25) & =0.\end{aligned}
$$

The auxiliary equation is therefore

$$
\begin{aligned}{\lambda }^{2}+10\lambda +25 & =0.\end{aligned}
$$

Factoring the auxiliary equation results in

$$
\begin{aligned}(\lambda +5)^{2} & =0\end{aligned}
$$

and so $\lambda =-5$ is a repeated root of the auxiliary equation.

Assuming $y={e}^{\lambda x}$ and differentiating $y$ with respect to $x$ gives

$$
{y}^{′}=\lambda {e}^{\lambda x},\,{y}^{″}={\lambda }^{2}{e}^{\lambda x}.
$$

Substituting the above into our differential equation gives

$$
\begin{aligned}{\lambda }^{2}{e}^{\lambda x}-6\lambda {e}^{\lambda x}+9{e}^{\lambda x} & =0 \\ {e}^{\lambda x}({\lambda }^{2}-6\lambda +9) & =0.\end{aligned}

extractions.name: Example: Finding General Solutions When the Characteristic Equation Has Repeated Roots
extractions.problem:
Find the general solution to the equation

$$
\frac{\textrm{d}^2 y}{\textrm{d} t^2} - 12\frac{\textrm{d} y}{\textrm{d} t} + 36y =0.
$$
extractions.worked_solution:
Assuming $y=e^{\lambda t}$ and differentiating $y$ with respect to $t$ gives

$$
\frac{\textrm{d} y}{\textrm{d} t}= \lambda e^{\lambda t},\qquad \frac{\textrm{d}^2 y}{\textrm{d} t^2}= \lambda^2 e^{\lambda t}.
$$

Substituting the above into our differential equation gives

$$
\begin{aligned}{\lambda }^{2}{e}^{\lambda t}-12\lambda {e}^{\lambda t}+36{e}^{\lambda t} & =0 \\ {e}^{\lambda t}({\lambda }^{2}-12\lambda +36) & =0.\end{aligned}
$$

The characteristic equation is 

$$
\begin{aligned}{\lambda }^{2}-12\lambda +36 & =0 \\ (\lambda -6)^{2} & =0,\end{aligned}
$$

and $\lambda =  6$ is a repeated root. Therefore, the general solution is

$$
y = Ae^{6 t} + Bte^{6t}.
$$

$$

extractions.worked_solution:
Let $y={e}^{\lambda x}.$ Differentiating $y$ with respect to $x$ gives

$$
\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}=\lambda {e}^{\lambda x},\,\frac{{\text{d}}^{2}y}{\text{d}{x}^{2}}={\lambda }^{2}{e}^{\lambda x}.
$$

Substituting the above into our differential equation gives

$$
\begin{aligned}{\lambda }^{2}{e}^{\lambda x}-3\lambda {e}^{\lambda x}+\frac{9}{4}{e}^{\lambda x} & =0 \\ {e}^{\lambda x}({\lambda }^{2}-3\lambda +\frac{9}{4}) & =0.\end{aligned}
$$

The auxiliary equation is therefore

$$
{\lambda }^{2}-3\lambda +\frac{9}{4}=0.
$$

Factoring the auxiliary equation gives

$$
\begin{aligned}(\lambda -\frac{3}{2})(\lambda -\frac{3}{2}) & =0 \\ {(\lambda -\frac{3}{2})}^{2} & =0.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, $\lambda =\frac{3}{2}$ is a repeated root.

So the general solution to the differential equation is

$$
y=A{e}^{3x/2}+Bx{e}^{3x/2}.
$$

extractions.problem:
Find the general solution to the equation

$$
\frac{{\text{d}}^{2}y}{\text{d}{x}^{2}}+4\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}+4y=0.
$$

extractions.worked_solution:
Let $y={e}^{\lambda x}.$ Differentiating $y$ with respect to $x$ gives

$$
\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}=\lambda {e}^{\lambda x},\,\frac{{\text{d}}^{2}y}{\text{d}{x}^{2}}={\lambda }^{2}{e}^{\lambda x}.
$$

Substituting the above into our differential equation gives

$$
\begin{aligned}{\lambda }^{2}{e}^{\lambda x}+4\lambda {e}^{\lambda x}+4{e}^{\lambda x} & =0 \\ {e}^{\lambda x}({\lambda }^{2}+4\lambda +4) & =0.\end{aligned}
$$

The auxiliary equation is therefore

$$
{\lambda }^{2}+4\lambda +4=0.
$$

Factoring the auxiliary equation gives

$$
\begin{aligned}(\lambda +2)(\lambda +2)=0 \\ (\lambda +2)^{2}=0.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, $\lambda =-2$ is a repeated root.

So the general solution to the differential equation is

$$
y=A{e}^{-2x}+Bx{e}^{-2x}.
$$

extractions.worked_solution:
Let $y={e}^{\lambda x}.$ Differentiating $y$ with respect to $x$ gives

$$
\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}=\lambda {e}^{\lambda x},\,\frac{{\text{d}}^{2}y}{\text{d}{x}^{2}}={\lambda }^{2}{e}^{\lambda x}.
$$

Substituting the above into our differential equation gives

$$
\begin{aligned}{\lambda }^{2}{e}^{\lambda x}-6\lambda {e}^{\lambda x}+9{e}^{\lambda x} & =0 \\ {e}^{\lambda x}({\lambda }^{2}-6\lambda +9) & =0.\end{aligned}
$$

The auxiliary equation is therefore

$$
{\lambda }^{2}-6\lambda +9=0.
$$

Factoring the auxiliary equation gives

$$
\begin{aligned}(\lambda -3)(\lambda -3) & =0 \\ (\lambda -3)^{2} & =0.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, $\lambda =3$ is a repeated root.

So the general solution to the differential equation is

$$
y=A{e}^{3x}+Bx{e}^{3x}.
$$

{\lambda }^{2}-6\lambda +9=0.
$$

Factoring the auxiliary equation gives

$$
\begin{aligned}(\lambda -3)(\lambda -3) & =0 \\ (\lambda -3)^{2} & =0.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, $\lambda =3$ is a repeated root.

So the general solution to the differential equation is

$$
y=A{e}^{3x}+Bx{e}^{3x}.
$$

extractions.worked_solution:
Let $y={e}^{\lambda x}.$ Differentiating $y$ with respect to $x$ gives

$$
\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}=\lambda {e}^{\lambda x},\,\frac{{\text{d}}^{2}y}{\text{d}{x}^{2}}={\lambda }^{2}{e}^{\lambda x}.
$$

Substituting the above into our differential equation gives

$$
\begin{aligned}{\lambda }^{2}{e}^{\lambda x}+\frac{3}{2}\lambda {e}^{\lambda x}+\frac{9}{16}{e}^{\lambda x} & =0 \\ {e}^{\lambda x}({\lambda }^{2}+\frac{3}{2}\lambda +\frac{9}{16}) & =0.\end{aligned}
$$

The auxiliary equation is therefore

$$
{\lambda }^{2}+\frac{3}{2}\lambda +\frac{9}{16}=0.
$$

Factoring the auxiliary equation gives

$$
\begin{aligned}(\lambda +\frac{3}{4})(\lambda +\frac{3}{4}) & =0 \\ {(\lambda +\frac{3}{4})}^{2} & =0.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, $\lambda =-\frac{3}{4}$ is a repeated root.

So the general solution to the differential equation is

$$
y=A{e}^{-3x/4}+Bx{e}^{-3x/4}.
$$

$$
\frac{{\text{d}}^{2}y}{\text{d}{x}^{2}}+\frac{3}{2}\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}+\frac{9}{16}y=0.
$$

extractions.worked_solution:
Let $y={e}^{\lambda x}.$ Differentiating $y$ with respect to $x$ gives

$$
\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}=\lambda {e}^{\lambda x},\,\frac{{\text{d}}^{2}y}{\text{d}{x}^{2}}={\lambda }^{2}{e}^{\lambda x}.
$$

Substituting the above into our differential equation gives

$$
\begin{aligned}{\lambda }^{2}{e}^{\lambda x}+8\lambda {e}^{\lambda x}+16{e}^{\lambda x} & =0 \\ {e}^{\lambda x}({\lambda }^{2}+8\lambda +16) & =0.\end{aligned}
$$

The auxiliary equation is therefore

$$
{\lambda }^{2}+8\lambda +16=0.
$$

Factoring the auxiliary equation gives

$$
\begin{aligned}(\lambda +4)(\lambda +4) & =0 \\ (\lambda +4)^{2} & =0.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, $\lambda =-4$ is a repeated root.

So the general solution to the differential equation is

$$
y=A{e}^{-4x}+Bx{e}^{-4x}.
$$

extractions.problem:
Find the general solution to the equation

$$
\frac{{\text{d}}^{2}y}{\text{d}{x}^{2}}-5\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}+\frac{25y}{4}=0.
$$

extractions.worked_solution:
Let $y={e}^{\lambda x}.$ Differentiating $y$ with respect to $x$ gives

$$
\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}=\lambda {e}^{\lambda x},\,\frac{{\text{d}}^{2}y}{\text{d}{x}^{2}}={\lambda }^{2}{e}^{\lambda x}.
$$

Substituting the above into our differential equation gives

$$
\begin{aligned}{\lambda }^{2}{e}^{\lambda x}-5\lambda {e}^{\lambda x}+\frac{25}{4}{e}^{\lambda x} & =0 \\ {e}^{\lambda x}({\lambda }^{2}-5\lambda +\frac{25}{4}) & =0.\end{aligned}
$$

The auxiliary equation is therefore

$$
{\lambda }^{2}-5\lambda +\frac{25}{4}=0.
$$

Factoring the auxiliary equation gives

$$
\begin{aligned}(\lambda -\frac{5}{2})(\lambda -\frac{5}{2}) & =0 \\ {(\lambda -\frac{5}{2})}^{2} & =0.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, $\lambda =\frac{5}{2}$ is a repeated root.

So the general solution to the differential equation is

$$
y=A{e}^{5x/2}+Bx{e}^{5x/2}.
$$

extractions.worked_solution:
Let $y={e}^{\lambda x}.$ Differentiating $y$ with respect to $x$ gives

$$
\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}=\lambda {e}^{\lambda x},\,\frac{{\text{d}}^{2}y}{\text{d}{x}^{2}}={\lambda }^{2}{e}^{\lambda x}.
$$

Substituting the above into our differential equation gives

$$
\begin{aligned}{\lambda }^{2}{e}^{\lambda x}+18\lambda {e}^{\lambda x}+81{e}^{\lambda x} & =0 \\ {e}^{\lambda x}({\lambda }^{2}+18\lambda +81) & =0.\end{aligned}
$$

The auxiliary equation is therefore

$$
{\lambda }^{2}+18\lambda +81=0.
$$

Factoring the auxiliary equation gives

$$
\begin{aligned}(\lambda +9)(\lambda +9) & =0 \\ (\lambda +9)^{2} & =0.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, $\lambda =-9$ is a repeated root.

So the general solution to the differential equation is

$$
y=A{e}^{-9x}+Bx{e}^{-9x}.
$$

extractions.problem:
Find the general solution to the equation

$$
\frac{{\text{d}}^{2}y}{\text{d}{x}^{2}}-14\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}+49y=0.
$$

extractions.worked_solution:
Let $y={e}^{\lambda x}.$ Differentiating $y$ with respect to $x$ gives

$$
\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}=\lambda {e}^{\lambda x},\,\frac{{\text{d}}^{2}y}{\text{d}{x}^{2}}={\lambda }^{2}{e}^{\lambda x}.
$$

Substituting the above into our differential equation gives

$$
\begin{aligned}{\lambda }^{2}{e}^{\lambda x}-14\lambda {e}^{\lambda x}+49{e}^{\lambda x} & =0 \\ {e}^{\lambda x}({\lambda }^{2}-14\lambda +49) & =0.\end{aligned}
$$

The auxiliary equation is therefore

$$
{\lambda }^{2}-14\lambda +49=0.
$$

Factoring the auxiliary equation gives

$$
\begin{aligned}(\lambda -7)(\lambda -7) & =0 \\ (\lambda -7)^{2} & =0.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, $\lambda =7$ is a repeated root.

So the general solution to the differential equation is

$$
y=A{e}^{7x}+Bx{e}^{7x}.
$$

extractions.problem:
Find the general solution to the equation

$$
\frac{{\text{d}}^{2}y}{\text{d}{x}^{2}}-2\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}+y=0.
$$

extractions.worked_solution:
Let $y={e}^{\lambda x}.$ Differentiating $y$ with respect to $x$ gives

$$
\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}=\lambda {e}^{\lambda x},\,\frac{{\text{d}}^{2}y}{\text{d}{x}^{2}}={\lambda }^{2}{e}^{\lambda x}.
$$

Substituting the above into our differential equation gives

$$
\begin{aligned}{\lambda }^{2}{e}^{\lambda x}-2\lambda {e}^{\lambda x}+{e}^{\lambda x} & =0 \\ {e}^{\lambda x}({\lambda }^{2}-2\lambda +1) & =0.\end{aligned}
$$

The auxiliary equation is therefore

$$
{\lambda }^{2}-2\lambda +1=0.
$$

Factoring the auxiliary equation gives

$$
\begin{aligned}(\lambda -1)^{2}=0.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, $\lambda =1$ is a repeated root.

So the general solution to the differential equation is

$$
y=A{e}^{x}+Bx{e}^{x}.
$$

extractions.name: Example: Identifying Non-Solutions of Second-Order Homogeneous ODEs
extractions.problem:
Given the equation $y''+12y'+36y = 0$  for $y=y(x),$ which of the following is **not** a solution to this equation?

I. $xe^{-6x}$

II. $4e^{-6x}-3xe^{-6x}$

III. $2e^{6x}$
extractions.worked_solution:
Assuming $y=e^{\lambda x}$ and differentiating $y$ with respect to $x$ gives

$$
y'= \lambda e^{\lambda x},\qquad y''= \lambda^2 e^{\lambda x}.
$$

Substituting the above into our differential equation gives

$$
\begin{aligned}{\lambda }^{2}{e}^{\lambda x}+12\lambda {e}^{\lambda x}+36{e}^{\lambda x} & =0 \\ {e}^{\lambda x}({\lambda }^{2}+12\lambda +36) & =0.\end{aligned}
$$

The characteristic equation is therefore

$$
\begin{aligned}{\lambda }^{2}+12\lambda +36 & =0 \\ (\lambda +6)^{2} & =0,\end{aligned}
$$

and $\lambda =-6$ is a repeated root.  Therefore, the general solution is

$$
y = Ae^{-6 x} + Bxe^{-6x}.
$$

Finally, we need to determine whether each of the given functions takes the form shown above.

- Function I takes the above form with $A=0$ and $B=1.$ So, it is a solution to the given ODE.

- Function II takes the above form with $A=4$ and $B=-3.$ So, it is a solution to the given ODE.

- Function III does *not* take the above form. It contains $e^{6x},$ which is not included in the above form. So, it is *not* a solution to the given ODE.

Therefore, the correct answer is "III only".

extractions.problem: Given the equation ${y}^{″}-14{y}^{′}+49y=0$ for $y=y(t),$ which of the following is **not** a solution to this equation?

extractions.worked_solution:
Assuming $y={e}^{\lambda t}$ and differentiating $y$ with respect to $t$ gives

$$
{y}^{′}=\lambda {e}^{\lambda t},\,{y}^{″}={\lambda }^{2}{e}^{\lambda t}.
$$

Substituting the above into our differential equation gives

$$
\begin{aligned}{\lambda }^{2}{e}^{\lambda t}-14\lambda {e}^{\lambda t}+49{e}^{\lambda t} & =0 \\ {e}^{\lambda t}({\lambda }^{2}-14\lambda +49) & =0.\end{aligned}
$$

The auxiliary equation is therefore

$$
\begin{aligned}{\lambda }^{2}-14\lambda +49 & =0.\end{aligned}
$$

Factoring the auxiliary equation results in

$$
\begin{aligned}(\lambda -7)^{2} & =0\end{aligned}
$$

and so $\lambda =7$ is a repeated root of the auxiliary equation.

Therefore, any linear combination of the functions ${e}^{7t}$ and $t{e}^{7t}$ is a solution to the original differential equation. 

Among the given options, only $7{e}^{t}+t{e}^{7t}$ is not a solution.

extractions.worked_solution:
Assuming $y={e}^{\lambda x}$ and differentiating $y$ with respect to $x$ gives

$$
{y}^{′}=\lambda {e}^{\lambda x},\,{y}^{″}={\lambda }^{2}{e}^{\lambda x}.
$$

Substituting the above into our differential equation gives

$$
\begin{aligned}{\lambda }^{2}{e}^{\lambda x}+10\lambda {e}^{\lambda x}+25{e}^{\lambda x} & =0 \\ {e}^{\lambda x}({\lambda }^{2}+10\lambda +25) & =0.\end{aligned}
$$

The auxiliary equation is therefore

$$
\begin{aligned}{\lambda }^{2}+10\lambda +25 & =0.\end{aligned}
$$

Factoring the auxiliary equation results in

$$
\begin{aligned}(\lambda +5)^{2} & =0\end{aligned}
$$

and so $\lambda =-5$ is a repeated root of the auxiliary equation.

Therefore, any linear combination of the functions ${e}^{-5x}$ and $x{e}^{-5x}$ is a solution to the original differential equation. 

Among the given options, only $10{e}^{5x}+3{e}^{-5x}$ is not a solution.

extractions.problem: Given the equation ${y}^{″}+4{y}^{′}+4y=0$ for $y=y(x),$ which of the following is **not** a solution to this equation?

extractions.worked_solution:
Assuming $y={e}^{\lambda x}$ and differentiating $y$ with respect to $x$ gives

$$
{y}^{′}=\lambda {e}^{\lambda x},\,{y}^{″}={\lambda }^{2}{e}^{\lambda x}.
$$

Substituting the above into our differential equation gives

$$
\begin{aligned}{\lambda }^{2}{e}^{\lambda x}+4\lambda {e}^{\lambda x}+4{e}^{\lambda x} & =0 \\ {e}^{\lambda x}({\lambda }^{2}+4\lambda +4) & =0.\end{aligned}
$$

The auxiliary equation is therefore

$$
\begin{aligned}{\lambda }^{2}+4\lambda +4 & =0.\end{aligned}
$$

Factoring the auxiliary equation results in

$$
\begin{aligned}(\lambda +2)^{2} & =0\end{aligned}
$$

and so $\lambda =-2$ is a repeated root of the auxiliary equation.

Therefore, any linear combination of the functions ${e}^{-2x}$ and $x{e}^{-2x}$ is a solution to the original differential equation. 

Among the given options, only $4{e}^{-x}$ is not a solution.

extractions.worked_solution:
Assuming $y={e}^{\lambda x}$ and differentiating $y$ with respect to $x$ gives

$$
{y}^{′}=\lambda {e}^{\lambda x},\,{y}^{″}={\lambda }^{2}{e}^{\lambda x}.
$$

Substituting the above into our differential equation gives

$$
\begin{aligned}{\lambda }^{2}{e}^{\lambda x}-8\lambda {e}^{\lambda x}+16{e}^{\lambda x} & =0 \\ {e}^{\lambda x}({\lambda }^{2}-8\lambda +16) & =0.\end{aligned}
$$

The auxiliary equation is therefore

$$
\begin{aligned}{\lambda }^{2}-8\lambda +16 & =0.\end{aligned}
$$

Factoring the auxiliary equation results in

$$
\begin{aligned}{(\lambda -4)}^{2} & =0\end{aligned}
$$

and so $\lambda =4$ is a repeated root of the auxiliary equation.

Therefore, any linear combination of the functions ${e}^{4x}$ and $x{e}^{4x}$ is a solution to the original differential equation. 

Among the given options, only $2{e}^{4x}+{e}^{-4x}$ is not a solution.

extractions.worked_solution:
Assuming $y={e}^{\lambda x}$ and differentiating $y$ with respect to $x$ gives

$$
{y}^{′}=\lambda {e}^{\lambda x},\,{y}^{″}={\lambda }^{2}{e}^{\lambda x}.
$$

Substituting the above into our differential equation gives

$$
\begin{aligned}{\lambda }^{2}{e}^{\lambda x}+3\lambda {e}^{\lambda x}+\frac{9}{4}{e}^{\lambda x} & =0 \\ {e}^{\lambda x}({\lambda }^{2}+3\lambda +\frac{9}{4}) & =0.\end{aligned}
$$

The auxiliary equation is therefore

$$
\begin{aligned}{\lambda }^{2}+3\lambda +\frac{9}{4} & =0.\end{aligned}
$$

Factoring the auxiliary equation results in

$$
\begin{aligned}{(\lambda +\frac{3}{2})}^{2} & =0\end{aligned}
$$

and so $\lambda =-\frac{3}{2}$ is a repeated root of the auxiliary equation.

Therefore, any linear combination of the functions ${e}^{-3x/2}$ and $x{e}^{-3x/2}$ is a solution to the original differential equation. 

Among the given options, only $x{e}^{-3x/2}-3{x}^{2}{e}^{-3x/2}$ is not a solution.

extractions.worked_solution:
Assuming $y={e}^{\lambda x}$ and differentiating $y$ with respect to $x$ gives

$$
{y}^{′}=\lambda {e}^{\lambda x},\,{y}^{″}={\lambda }^{2}{e}^{\lambda x}.
$$

Substituting the above into our differential equation gives

$$
\begin{aligned}{\lambda }^{2}{e}^{\lambda x}+6\lambda {e}^{\lambda x}+9{e}^{\lambda x} & =0 \\ {e}^{\lambda x}({\lambda }^{2}+6\lambda +9) & =0.\end{aligned}
$$

The auxiliary equation is therefore

$$
\begin{aligned}{\lambda }^{2}+6\lambda +9 & =0.\end{aligned}
$$

Factoring the auxiliary equation results in

$$
\begin{aligned}{(\lambda +3)}^{2} & =0\end{aligned}
$$

and so $\lambda =-3$ is a repeated root of the auxiliary equation.

Therefore, any linear combination of the functions ${e}^{-3x}$ and $x{e}^{-3x}$ is a solution to the original differential equation. 

Among the given options, only $2{e}^{-3x}+3x$ is not a solution.

extractions.problem: Given the equation ${y}^{″}-16{y}^{′}+64y=0$ for $y=y(x),$ which of the following is **not** a solution to this equation?

extractions.worked_solution:
Assuming $y={e}^{\lambda x}$ and differentiating $y$ with respect to $x$ gives

$$
{y}^{′}=\lambda {e}^{\lambda x},\,{y}^{″}={\lambda }^{2}{e}^{\lambda x}.
$$

Substituting the above into our differential equation gives

$$
\begin{aligned}{\lambda }^{2}{e}^{\lambda x}-16\lambda {e}^{\lambda x}+64{e}^{\lambda x} & =0 \\ {e}^{\lambda x}({\lambda }^{2}-16\lambda +64) & =0.\end{aligned}
$$

The auxiliary equation is therefore

$$
\begin{aligned}{\lambda }^{2}-16\lambda +64 & =0.\end{aligned}
$$

Factoring the auxiliary equation results in

$$
\begin{aligned}{(\lambda -8)}^{2} & =0\end{aligned}
$$

and so $\lambda =8$ is a repeated root of the auxiliary equation.

Therefore, any linear combination of the functions ${e}^{8x}$ and $x{e}^{8x}$ is a solution to the original differential equation. 

Among the given options, only ${x}^{2}{e}^{8x}$ is not a solution.

extractions.problem: Given the equation ${y}^{″}-10{y}^{′}+25y=0$ for $y=y(x),$ which of the following is **not** a solution to this equation?

extractions.worked_solution:
Assuming $y={e}^{\lambda x}$ and differentiating $y$ with respect to $x$ gives

$$
{y}^{′}=\lambda {e}^{\lambda x},\,{y}^{″}={\lambda }^{2}{e}^{\lambda x}.
$$

Substituting the above into our differential equation gives

$$
\begin{aligned}{\lambda }^{2}{e}^{\lambda x}-10\lambda {e}^{\lambda x}+25{e}^{\lambda x} & =0 \\ {e}^{\lambda x}({\lambda }^{2}-10\lambda +25) & =0.\end{aligned}
$$

The auxiliary equation is therefore

$$
\begin{aligned}{\lambda }^{2}-10\lambda +25 & =0.\end{aligned}
$$

Factoring the auxiliary equation results in

$$
\begin{aligned}(\lambda -5)^{2} & =0\end{aligned}
$$

and so $\lambda =5$ is a repeated root of the auxiliary equation.

Therefore, any linear combination of the functions ${e}^{5x}$ and $x{e}^{5x}$ is a solution to the original differential equation. 

Among the given options, only ${e}^{5x}-5{e}^{x}$ is not a solution.

extractions.problem: Given the equation ${y}^{″}+\frac{1}{2}{y}^{′}+\frac{1}{16}y=0$ for $y=y(x),$ which of the following is **not** a solution to this equation?

extractions.worked_solution:
Assuming $y={e}^{\lambda x}$ and differentiating $y$ with respect to $x$ gives

$$
{y}^{′}=\lambda {e}^{\lambda x},\,{y}^{″}={\lambda }^{2}{e}^{\lambda x}.
$$

Substituting the above into our differential equation gives

$$
\begin{aligned}{\lambda }^{2}{e}^{\lambda x}+\frac{1}{2}\lambda {e}^{\lambda x}+\frac{1}{16}{e}^{\lambda x} & =0 \\ {e}^{\lambda x}({\lambda }^{2}+\frac{1}{2}\lambda +\frac{1}{16}) & =0.\end{aligned}
$$

The auxiliary equation is therefore

$$
\begin{aligned}{\lambda }^{2}+\frac{1}{2}\lambda +\frac{1}{16} & =0.\end{aligned}
$$

Factoring the auxiliary equation results in

$$
\begin{aligned}{(\lambda +\frac{1}{4})}^{2} & =0\end{aligned}
$$

and so $\lambda =-\frac{1}{4}$ is a repeated root of the auxiliary equation.

Therefore, any linear combination of the functions ${e}^{-x/4}$ and $x{e}^{-x/4}$ is a solution to the original differential equation. 

Among the given options, only $2{e}^{-4x}+3x{e}^{-x/4}$ is not a solution.

extractions.problem: Given the equation ${y}^{″}-18{y}^{′}+81y=0$ for $y=y(t),$ which of the following is **not** a solution to this equation?

extractions.worked_solution:
Assuming $y={e}^{\lambda t}$ and differentiating $y$ with respect to $t$ gives

$$
{y}^{′}=\lambda {e}^{\lambda t},\,{y}^{″}={\lambda }^{2}{e}^{\lambda t}.
$$

Substituting the above into our differential equation gives

$$
\begin{aligned}{\lambda }^{2}{e}^{\lambda t}-18\lambda {e}^{\lambda t}+81{e}^{\lambda t} & =0 \\ {e}^{\lambda t}({\lambda }^{2}-18\lambda +81) & =0.\end{aligned}
$$

The auxiliary equation is therefore

$$
\begin{aligned}{\lambda }^{2}-18\lambda +81 & =0.\end{aligned}
$$

Factoring the auxiliary equation results in

$$
\begin{aligned}(\lambda -9)^{2} & =0\end{aligned}
$$

and so $\lambda =9$ is a repeated root of the auxiliary equation.

Therefore, any linear combination of the functions ${e}^{9t}$ and $t{e}^{9t}$ is a solution to the original differential equation. 

Among the given options, only $3{e}^{-9t}$ is not a solution.
